item.title: SQL Server String Concatenation Across Rows: Why Variable Assignment Fails and Guaranteed Alternatives
item.description:
“SQL Server String Concatenation Across Rows: Why Variable Assignment Fails and Guaranteed Alternatives”

Why do traditional SQL Server queries relying on sequential variable assignment (e.g., @variable = @variable + [column]) for concatenating strings from multiple rows often produce inconsistent or incorrect results, particularly when an ORDER BY clause is involved? How can developers ensure reliable, ordered string aggregation in T-SQL across different server versions?

The core issue stems from SQL being fundamentally a set-manipulation language, not a procedural scripting environment. The order of execution for expressions within the SELECT list, especially when involving self-referencing variable assignments like @a = @a + [msg], is not guaranteed to align with the ordering dictated by the ORDER BY clause.

item.title: SQL Server: Retrieve Last Inserted Identity Value Safely
item.description:
“SQL Server: Retrieve Last Inserted Identity Value Safely”

Methods for Retrieving the Last Inserted Identity Value

Several T-SQL functions and clauses are designed for this purpose. Let’s examine them:

1. @@IDENTITY

This global variable returns the last identity value generated for any table in the current session, across all scopes.

  • Caveat: Its primary drawback is that it’s not scope-specific. If a trigger fires during your insert and that trigger also inserts into an identity column, @@IDENTITY will return the identity value from the trigger’s insert, not your original statement. This can lead to unexpected results and errors.

2. SCOPE_IDENTITY()

This function is generally considered the most robust and recommended method. It returns the last identity value generated for any table within the current session and, critically, within the current scope.
